claims.claim: Activation of TLR7 at the epithelial barrier of the skin and gut launches a specific and distinct monopoiesis response which does not occur after systemic TLR7 activation or activation of other TLRs.
claims.source: Herein, we demonstrate that activation of TLR7 at the epithelial barrier of the skin and gut launches a specific and distinct monopoiesis response which does not occur after systemic TLR7 activation or activation of other TLRs.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: The TLR7-induced monocytes appear to be immature and programmed to differentiate into macrophages.
claims.source: It is characterised by a rapid and dramatic increase of blood monocytes that egress from the BM bypassing the requirement of homeostatic cues like CCR2 or CX3CR1. The TLR7-induced monocytes appear to be immature and programmed to differentiate into macrophages, both surveying the endothelial integrity as Ly6C-low monocytes and trans-migrating into different organs to complement tissue resident macrophages.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from phenotyping and tissue infiltration experiments.

claims.claim: The response is orchestrated by BM-derived myeloid cells capable of transmitting the signals to the BM HSPCs independently from some of the well-known cytokines such type I and type II IFNs.
claims.source: The response is orchestrated by BM-derived myeloid cells capable of transmitting the signals to the BM HSPCs independently from some of the well-known cytokines such type I and type II IFNs (summarised in Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from chimera and cytokine blocking experiments.

claims.claim: These findings define the unique features of the BM myeloid response triggered by single-stranded RNA viruses on entering the epithelial barrier.
claims.source: Collectively our findings define the unique features of the BM myeloid response triggered by single-stranded RNA viruses on entering the epithelial barrier, a condition most likely occurring in infections with arboviruses and coronaviruses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claims.claim: The canonical role of TLR7 in sensing viral ssRNA makes it evolutionarily logical for the response to be specific to epithelial barriers.
claims.source: Although the detailed mechanisms underlying this specificity remain to be defined, the canonical role of TLR7 in sensing viral ssRNA makes it evolutionarily logical for the response to be specific to epithelial barriers, which must be breached for infection to be established.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary logic of the findings.

claims.claim: In the skin and gut, a subset of macrophages are replenished by circulating monocytes.
claims.source: Notably, in the skin and gut a subset of macrophages are replenished by circulating monocytes (Bain et al., 2014; Kolter et al., 2019), unlike in other tissues where macrophages are embryonically derived, proliferate in situ and are only replenished by circulating monocytes after a severe insult (Ginhoux and Guilliams, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the TLR7.1 transgenic mouse, the monocyte response appears to be driven by the extramedullary haematopoiesis in the spleen.
claims.source: Interestingly, TLR7 hyperactivation has been shown to drive a myeloid cell expansion in other settings, such as the transgenic overexpression of TLR7 in the TLR7.1 mouse (Deane et al., 2007). However, in these models the monocyte response appears to be driven by the extramedullary haematopoiesis in the spleen, whilst in our experimental model the BM is the only source of the myeloid expansion demonstrating the specificity of the peripheral cues induced by TLR7 activation in the skin and gut.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to published data supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The monocytosis following topical R848 applications is accompanied by a dramatic expansion of HSPCs and monocyte progenitor cells in the BM.
claims.source: The monocytosis following topical R848 applications is accompanied by a dramatic expansion of HSPCs and monocyte progenitor cells in the BM and the egression in the peripheral blood of transitional BM pre-monocytes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from BRDU incorporation experiments.

claims.claim: The expanded BM monocyte population expressed high levels of Sca-1, consistent with previous reports of emergency myelopoiesis.
claims.source: In concordance with previous reports, we found that the expanded BM monocyte population expressed high levels of Sca-1 (Askenase et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and a citation.

claims.claim: The induced monocytosis was independent of both type I and type II IFNs.
claims.source: However, in our model the induced monocytosis was independent of both type I and type II IFNs, indicating that a different priming mechanism had occurred.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments with IFN knockout mice.

claims.claim: Type III IFN may have a still unrecognized role in the regulation of monocyte progenitors.
claims.source: One interesting possibility is the type III IFN, which is increasingly recognised as an inducer of local antiviral immunity at epithelial barriers (Lazear et al., 2015; Wack et al., 2015) and may have a still unrecognised role in the regulation of monocyte progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claims.claim: CSF-1 signalling may be involved in the monocyte expansion observed in the experimental model.
claims.source: It is also possible that CSF-1 signalling is involved in the monocyte expansion observed in our experimental model, given the upregulation of the CSF1R (CD115) on the R848-expanded monocytes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed upregulation of CD115.

claims.claim: TLR7 activation of Ly6C-high monocytes using topical IMQ or in vitro can directly promote their conversion to Ly6C-low monocytes.
claims.source: Recent work has suggested that TLR7 activation of Ly6C-high monocytes using topical IMQ or in vitro can directly promote their conversion to Ly6C-low monocytes (Gamrekelashvili et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a reference to published work supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The accelerated monocyte conversion after topical TLR7 activation appears to be an indirect effect driven by a secondary stimulus.
claims.source: However, while we agree that topical TLR7 activation can accelerate monocyte conversion, this appears to be an indirect effect driven by a secondary stimulus, as IV or IP administration of R848 did not result in an obvious monocyte ratio switch.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of different routes of administration.

claims.claim: The BM egression of monocytes in steady-steady conditions and during emergency myelopoiesis in response to inflammation and/or infections has been reported to depend on CCR2 expression.
claims.source: The BM egression of monocytes in steady-steady conditions and during emergency myelopoiesis in response to inflammation and/or infections, including Toxoplasma gondii and Listeria monocytogenes, has been reported to depend on CCR2 expression (Grainger et al., 2013; Serbina and Pamer, 2006; Serbina et al., 2009) and this has become an accepted dogma in the literature.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Topical TLR7 application generates monocytes which are released from the BM in a CCR2-independent process.
claims.source: However, our findings demonstrate unequivocally that topical TLR7 application generates monocytes which are released from the BM in a CCR2-independent process.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments with CCR2 knockout mice.

claims.claim: During La Crosse virus infection, monocyte egression occurs in a CCR2-independent manner.
claims.source: To our knowledge, the only other context in which this has been shown is during La Crosse virus infection, which interestingly has an ssRNA genome and is detected via TLR7 (Winkler et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a reference to published work supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The R848-induced peripheral blood monocytes have low CCR2 expression and have an immature CXCR4-high, F4/80-low phenotype reminiscent of BM pre-monocytes.
claims.source: Consistent with a CCR2-independent egress, the R848-induced peripheral blood monocytes have low CCR2 expression and have an immature CXCR4-high, F4/80-low phenotype reminiscent of BM pre-monocytes (Chong et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and a citation.

claims.claim: Under homeostatic conditions, CXCR4 and CCR2 play antagonistic roles dictating the respective retention or release of Ly6C-high monocytes from the BM.
claims.source: Under homeostatic conditions, CXCR4 and CCR2 play antagonistic roles dictating the respective retention or release of Ly6C-high monocytes from the BM (Jung et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The presence of upregulated CXCR4 on blood monocytes potentially indicates their premature release to meet increased demand via a bypass of the CCR2/CXCR4 axis.
claims.source: Therefore, the presence of upregulated CXCR4 on blood monocytes potentially indicates their premature release to meet increased demand via a bypass of the CCR2/CXCR4 axis.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phenotype.

claims.claim: A potentially similar phenomenon of premature monocyte release has been suggested during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: Of note, a potentially similar phenomenon has been suggested during SARS-CoV-2 infection, based on the presence of proliferation markers on blood monocytes (Mann et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a reference to published work supported by a citation.

claims.claim: An early recruitment of Ly6C-high monocytes into the lung is a beneficial feature of the host innate immune response to virus infection.
claims.source: Consistent with the notion and previous data (Goritzka et al., 2015) that an early recruitment of Ly6C-high monocytes into the lung is a beneficial feature of the host innate immune response to virus infection, we found that the influx of R848-induced emergency myeloid cells restricted RSV and influenza virus replication and dampened disease severity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by viral infection experiments and a citation.

claims.claim: Monocyte-derived cells have been shown to limit HSV-2 and HSV-1 replication in the vaginal tract and in the cornea, respectively.
claims.source: Similarly, monocyte-derived cells have been shown to limit HSV-2 and HSV-1 replication in the vaginal tract and in the cornea, respectively (Conrady et al., 2013; Iijima et al., 2011), indicating that these cells play a key role in the resistance to viruses together with the type I IFNs.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The monocytosis persisted long after the TLR7 stimulation at the epithelial barrier had ceased.
claims.source: Notably, the fact that the monocytosis persisted long after the TLR7 stimulation at the epithelial barrier had ceased would suggest that the protective effects provided by these cells may prolong the antiviral effect of the type I IFNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the time course data showing prolonged monocytosis.

claims.claim: The protective effects provided by the R848-induced monocytes may prolong the antiviral effect of the type I IFNs.
claims.source: Notably, the fact that the monocytosis persisted long after the TLR7 stimulation at the epithelial barrier had ceased would suggest that the protective effects provided by these cells may prolong the antiviral effect of the type I IFNs.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed persistence of monocytosis.

claims.claim: Inflammatory Ly6C-high monocytes have been shown to contribute to lung pathology in a model of influenza virus infection.
claims.source: However, blood-derived tissue macrophages can also induce tissue damage. For example, inflammatory Ly6C-high monocytes have been shown to contribute to lung pathology in a model of influenza virus infection (Davidson et al., 2014; Herold et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2008), most likely recapitulating the pathology that occurs in severe infection if the initial innate response is dysregulated.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dynamic changes in the monocyte response have been correlated with COVID-19 disease severity during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: A similar pattern has also been reported during SARS-CoV-2 infection where dynamic changes in the monocyte response have been correlated with COVID-19 disease severity (Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Recruitment of antiviral monocytes during lung infections must be carefully balanced to reduce viral load but not allow excessive cell infiltration that can cause tissue damage.
claims.source: Therefore, recruitment of antiviral monocytes during lung infections must be carefully balanced to reduce viral load but not allow excessive cell infiltration that can cause tissue damage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of beneficial and harmful effects of monocytes.

claims.claim: The work presented elucidates a novel pathway of emergency myelopoiesis which is uniquely activated by TLR7-expressing macrophages at epithelial barriers.
claims.source: In summary, the work presented here elucidates a novel pathway of emergency myelopoiesis which is uniquely activated by TLR7-expressing macrophages at epithelial barriers.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claims.claim: This emergency myeloid population is pushed towards a macrophage differentiation pathway which results in a predominance of Ly6C-low patrolling monocytes in the blood and a simultaneous infiltration of inflammatory macrophages into peripheral organs.
claims.source: This emergency myeloid population is pushed towards a macrophage differentiation pathway which results in a predominance of Ly6C-low patrolling monocytes in the blood and a simultaneous infiltration of inflammatory macrophages into peripheral organs.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: These data challenge the dogma on how monocytes are produced during viral infections occurring at peripheral sites.
claims.source: Together these data challenge the dogma on how monocytes are produced during viral infections occurring at peripheral sites and highlight their contribution to the initial antiviral immunity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

results.result: Topical R848 administration at epithelial barriers induces a marked monocytosis (~30-fold expansion) with a ratio switch toward Ly6C-low monocytes (>90% of total monocytes). This response is specific to topical/oral routes and is dose-dependent, requiring potent TLR7 agonism.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 provide quantitative flow cytometry data showing the 30-fold monocyte expansion and >90% Ly6C-low predominance. Claims C29-C30 demonstrate route specificity (topical/oral vs IV/IP), and C32-C33 establish dose-dependence with appropriate controls. The data are internally consistent and supported by multiple independent experiments with statistical significance.

results.result: The monocytosis response is unique to TLR7 activation, as other TLR agonists (LPS, poly I:C, CpG) and pro-inflammatory stimuli (TPA) failed to induce similar effects. TLR7 knockout mice showed no response, confirming pathway specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate negative results with multiple TLR agonists using appropriate controls. C38-C39 provide genetic validation through Tlr7-/- mice showing complete loss of response. The specificity is well-established through systematic comparison of multiple stimuli with consistent negative controls.

results.result: The TLR7-induced monocytosis occurs independently of canonical CCR2/CX3CR1 axes and prototypical cytokines (IFN-γ, type I IFN, IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 demonstrate independence from multiple cytokine pathways using knockout mice and blocking antibodies. However, the mechanistic basis for this independence remains unclear, and the authors acknowledge in the limitations that the soluble mediator remains unidentified. While the negative results are convincing, the lack of a positive mechanism weakens the overall understanding.

results.result: Bone marrow-derived myeloid cells, specifically Lyz2-expressing cells, orchestrate the monocyte response. Lymphocytes, eosinophils, mast cells, basophils, and neutrophils are dispensable, and skin monocyte infiltration suggests a positive feedback mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C54 use appropriate genetic models (BM chimeras, Rag2-/-, cell-specific knockouts, depletion studies) to exclude various cell types. However, C50 shows only 50% reduction in Lyz2Cre mice, indicating partial involvement. C57 proposes a positive feedback mechanism based solely on monocyte infiltration (C56) without mechanistic validation. The identity of the specific myeloid cell type and the feedback mechanism require further investigation.

results.result: The monocyte response originates from bone marrow emergency myelopoiesis, bypassing the splenic reservoir. R848 dramatically increases HSPC proliferation (~4.6% to ~45.6% in cell cycle) with specific expansion of monocyte progenitors (MDPs, cMoPs) but not granulocyte progenitors (GMPs).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 use splenectomy and lineage tracing to establish BM origin. C62-C65 provide BRDU incorporation data showing dramatic HSPC proliferation with lineage specificity. C66 shows Sca1 upregulation consistent with emergency myelopoiesis. C67 demonstrates prolonged monocytosis (17 days). The data are internally consistent and use appropriate experimental approaches, though the mechanism driving BM-specific response remains unclear.

results.result: R848-induced monocytes egress from bone marrow with an immature Ly6C-high profile and undergo accelerated differentiation into Ly6C-low monocytes and tissue macrophages in multiple organs (lung, liver, kidney). Depletion of Ly6C-high monocytes abrogates the entire monocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 provide strong evidence through depletion experiments that Ly6C-low cells derive from Ly6C-high precursors. C71-C73 demonstrate tissue infiltration through immunofluorescence with appropriate quantification. However, the claim of "accelerated" differentiation (C74) is inferred from the ratio switch and depletion data rather than directly measured through kinetic studies or single-cell tracking.

results.result: The TLR7-induced monocyte egression and tissue infiltration occur independently of CCR2 and CX3CR1, with CCR2-deficient mice showing even higher Ly6C-low fold increases. Vascular permeability is not increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 use appropriate knockout models (Ccr2RFP/RFP, Cx3cr1GFP/GFP) demonstrating monocytosis persists and is even enhanced in CCR2-deficient mice. C83-C84 use Evans Blue to rule out non-specific vascular permeability changes. This challenges established dogma (C114) and is well-supported, though the alternative egression mechanism remains unidentified.

results.result: R848-induced monocytes display an immature, activated phenotype with increased Sca1, CD115, CXCR4, CD11c, CD11a, CD62L and decreased F4/80, CCR2. This phenotype resembles transitional BM pre-monocytes, suggesting premature egress of an emergency population.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 provide comprehensive flow cytometry phenotyping showing consistent markers of immaturity and activation. C92 appropriately cites published data on pre-monocyte phenotypes for comparison. However, C93's conclusion of "premature egress" is speculative, based on phenotypic similarity rather than direct demonstration that these are indeed pre-monocytes released early. The interpretation is reasonable but not definitively proven.

results.result: R848-induced monocytes display a blunted cytokine response upon TLR7 restimulation but maintain normal responses to LPS, indicating pathway-specific adaptation or tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 demonstrate reduced cytokine production upon R848 rechallenge but normal LPS responses through in vitro restimulation experiments. This suggests trained immunity or tolerance. However, the mechanism underlying this adaptation is not explored, and it's unclear whether this represents epigenetic reprogramming of HSPCs or monocyte-intrinsic changes.

results.result: R848 pretreatment reduces lung viral load and disease severity after RSV and influenza virus infection, with decreased weight loss and reduced viral gene copies in lungs.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 provide viral load measurements (qPCR) and disease monitoring (weight loss) showing protective effects. However, the experiments lack mechanistic dissection—it's unclear whether protection is due to the monocytes themselves, their tissue macrophage derivatives, or indirect effects. Depletion experiments during viral challenge would strengthen causality. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=6-8) with statistical significance.

results.result: The kinetics of R848-induced monocytosis show initial leukopenia after one treatment, followed by rapid expansion of both monocyte subpopulations after two treatments, with continued Ly6C-low expansion and stable Ly6C-high levels on subsequent treatments. Neutrophils remain unchanged throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 provide detailed time-course data with appropriate controls. C28's inference that this indicates lack of pan-myeloid response is supported by C27's neutrophil data. The kinetics are well-characterized and internally consistent, providing important temporal resolution of the response.

results.result: The study defines a novel pathway of emergency myelopoiesis uniquely activated by TLR7 at epithelial barriers, characterized by CCR2-independent monocyte egression, accelerated macrophage differentiation, and BM-derived myeloid cell orchestration independent of type I/II IFNs. This challenges existing dogma on monocyte production during viral infections.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C100-C103, C128-C130) accurately synthesize the major findings supported by the grouped experimental results. The work does challenge established dogma about CCR2-dependence (C114-C115) with strong evidence. However, the mechanistic gaps (unidentified soluble mediator, specific myeloid cell type, feedback mechanism) prevent complete understanding of the pathway.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about monocyte biology, including their heterogeneity, CCR2-dependent egression, Ly6C subpopulations, patrolling behavior, TLR7 responsiveness, and roles in viral infections.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C13-C19, C105, C114, C118, C122, C125-C126) represent established knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. They provide necessary context for the experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: Intraperitoneal R848 administration at various doses (1, 10, 100 µg) did not cause significant increases in blood monocyte counts compared to vehicle.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 is supported by dose-response data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. This negative result is important for establishing route specificity and is appropriately controlled. The lack of response across a 100-fold dose range strengthens the conclusion that systemic administration is insufficient.

results.result: Speculative claims about evolutionary logic of barrier-specific responses, potential roles of type III IFN and CSF-1, comparison to other models (TLR7.1 mice, IMQ studies, La Crosse virus, SARS-CoV-2), and mechanisms of premature monocyte release.
results.evaluation: These claims (C104, C106, C110-C113, C116, C119-C120, C124) are explicitly speculative or comparative. C104 offers evolutionary reasoning without experimental support. C110-C111 propose type III IFN and CSF-1 involvement without testing. C112-C113 discuss published work on IMQ with different interpretations. C116, C120 cite relevant viral infection models. C119, C124 speculate on mechanisms. These are appropriate for discussion but lack experimental validation in this study.

results.result: Speculative mechanistic claims about splenic retention of monocytes, positive feedback by infiltrating myeloid cells, and premature egress of emergency populations based on phenotypic similarity to pre-monocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60, C57, C92-C93 are explicitly marked as speculation or suggestion in the evidence. C60 speculates about splenic retention based on enhanced phenotype in splenectomized mice. C57 proposes positive feedback based solely on infiltration without mechanistic validation. C92-C93 infer premature egress from phenotypic similarity to published pre-monocyte data. While reasonable hypotheses, these require experimental validation.

results.result: Comparative and contextual claims relating findings to published literature on emergency myelopoiesis, Sca-1 expression, IFN-independence, CCR2-independent egression, beneficial monocyte recruitment, persistence of monocytosis, and balanced immune responses.
results.evaluation: These claims (C108-C109, C115, C117, C121, C123, C127) appropriately contextualize the current findings within existing literature. C108 compares Sca-1 expression to published emergency myelopoiesis markers. C109, C115, C117 contrast with established mechanisms. C121, C123 relate to beneficial effects of monocytes. C127 synthesizes understanding of balanced responses. These are well-supported by both current data and appropriate citations.
